rv.q: Taylor's Richards is a hoot yet she almost gets upstaged by another character, which is hard to do in a one-woman show.
Ms. Taylor's lively, funny, humane Ann Richards looks mighty formidable, despite the unshaded if colorful writing and the slack direction.
The physical and spiritual illusion is so masterful that when a huge portrait of the real Richards appears at one point, it feels like a wasted effort.
Otherwise, this trip does not feel necessary.
Holland Taylor's one-woman show about the late Texas governor Ann Richards is a missed opportunity that feels more like a campaign speech than a play.
One might easily think that a solo show would be swallowed up on Theatre's largest stage, but given Richards' dynamism and Taylor's outsize talents, the ladies had no problem filling the space.
Taylor lays her out there, warts and all, with relish and consummate skill.
More conflict--and moods--would make this a better showcase, but if you miss the public spectacle that was Ann Richards, she's definitely back.
The show would also be better suited for a more intimate theater rather than the extended thrust stage of the Vivian Beamount at Lincoln Center.
Taylor is a pistol. She immerses herself deep into the role, conveying Richards' big-as-Texas appeal.
But this meandering hagiography unbecomes the swaggering doyenne who, for a time, outgunned the sharpshooters around her.
The best parts of the show come at the beginning and the end when Taylor is back at the front of the stage.
But a great dinner companion is not necessarily an ideal subject for a nearly two-hour play.
Just not enough of them to lasso our attention and really rope us in.
